title: Why caches work: latency, locality and hit ratios
goal: By the end, you can explain why a small copy of the data kept close by answers most requests, work out what a hit ratio means for the database behind it, and measure how big a cache must be.
opening:
Picture a busy café. The barista makes a latte every thirty seconds, and never walks to the storeroom for milk. A jug sits on the counter, and she goes to the back only when it runs out. Walking takes far longer than pouring.

The payments program behind the café's card reader faces the same choice thousands of times a second. For every tap, it needs the shop's details from a database on another computer. The usual fix is a copy kept close by. Once the copy answers 99 lookups in 100, the job feels done, because ninety-nine sounds nearly perfect. But the hundredth lookup still goes to the database, and decides how hard it works.

Running PostgreSQL, which ended the Storage engines track, showed that each connection costs a real database a whole process; here we stop asking it the same question over and over. In this lesson, we'll measure how far away data can be, see why a small copy catches most requests, and count what the misses cost. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments program keeps copies of shop details close by, in a cache. A lookup that finds its copy there takes 0.5 ms (thousandths of a second). One that doesn't has to ask the database, and takes 10 ms. Today, 99 of every 100 lookups find their copy. A change makes it 999 of every 1,000. What happens?
options: Lookups get about 1% faster on average, and the database gets about 1% fewer questions
Lookups get about 15% faster on average, and the database gets a tenth of the questions it got before
Lookups get about ten times faster on average, and the database's work barely changes
Nothing you could measure: past 99 in 100, a copy is as good as it gets
warmup.why: Work out the average. At 99 in 100, it's 0.99 × 0.5 + 0.01 × 10 = 0.595 ms. At 999 in 1,000, it's 0.5095 ms, about 14% less. The database only hears about the lookups the cache can't answer, and those fall from 1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000: a tenth of its work. The first option is the trap. It treats 99% and 99.9% as nearly the same number, which they are for the cache and aren't for the database. The third section builds this up, and the rest of the lesson asks why caches reach numbers like these at all.

sections.h: How far away the data is: a ladder from the CPU to another country
sections.body:
Let's start with one card payment. A customer taps a card at the café, and the payments program has to decide whether to trust it. That fraud check needs the shop's details: its name, its country and what kind of shop it is. The shops live in a table called `merchants` (the code's word for shops), in a database on another computer. A database is a program that stores records, in tables of rows, and answers questions about them.

Where could the shop's details be? If the program kept them in its own memory, in a `HashMap` from each shop's id to its details, a lookup would take about 100 nanoseconds. A nanosecond (ns) is a billionth of a second. From the database across the network, the same details are a millisecond or two away, more than ten thousand times further. Almost none of that time is work. It's distance: wires, other programs and queues between the program and the bytes.

Computers keep data in layers. The CPU, the chip that runs a program's instructions, has a few tiny memories of its own, called CPU caches. Next comes main memory, or RAM: much bigger, on separate chips, and wiped when the power goes off. Then the disk, which keeps data through a power cut. Each layer further from the CPU is bigger, cheaper per byte and slower. The figure shows this ladder, and the blue rungs were measured by this lesson's demo.

- A read from L1, the smallest and nearest CPU cache, takes about a nanosecond. L1 holds only 32 to 128 KB for each core (one of the CPU's processing units) on current CPUs.
- A read from RAM, when the data isn't in any CPU cache, takes about 100 ns.
- The operating system, the program that runs all the others, keeps recently read files in RAM, in its page cache. Reading 4 KB from there means asking the operating system and copying the bytes: about a microsecond (µs, a millionth of a second).
- A read from an SSD, the flash-memory disk in most computers today, takes tens of microseconds, up to about 0.1 ms.
- A round trip is a message to another machine and its answer back. Inside one data center (a building full of computers), it takes about 0.1 to 0.5 ms, before that machine does any work.
- A round trip to another region is limited by light in glass fiber, about 200,000 km a second. Amsterdam to New York is about 5,900 km, so the round trip can't take less than about 60 ms, and real routes make 70 to 150 ms common.

Each rung is ten to a thousand times slower than the one above it. That gap is why caches exist. The barista's jug is one. A **cache** is a smaller, faster store that keeps copies of some of the data from a bigger, slower one. A read that finds its data in the cache is a hit, and pays only for the fast rung. A read that doesn't is a miss: it pays for the slow rung, and usually leaves a copy behind for next time, the way the barista refills the jug.

Why not copy everything up a rung? Because the fast layers are small, and the data keeps changing. A server, a computer that runs programs for others over the network, has tens or hundreds of gigabytes of RAM, and the database behind it can hold terabytes. So a cache holds only part of the data. Next, we'll see why a small part goes a long way.

sections.h: A few shops get most of the lookups, so a small cache catches most of them
sections.body:
If every shop were equally popular, a cache would be a poor deal. Hold 10% of a million shops and you'd find the answer 10% of the time. Real traffic isn't like that. A supermarket chain's shop id turns up in thousands of payments a minute, and a bicycle repair shop's twice a day. Two habits of real traffic make caches pay.

The first is **locality**: programs tend to come back to data they used recently, and to data next to it. Coming back soon is called temporal locality. A customer who has paid once uses the same card again later that day, and a declined payment is often tried again within seconds. Reading the neighbors is called spatial locality. CPU caches bet on it by loading 64 bytes at a time, and databases by reading a whole 8 KB page, a fixed-size block of a file, at a time.

The second is **skew**: a few keys get most of the requests. A key is the name you look an item up by, here a shop's id. A common model of skew is the Zipf distribution, named after George Zipf, a linguist who saw that a few words make up most of what people say. Rank the keys by popularity, 1 for the most popular. The key of rank k gets a share of the requests in proportion to 1/k^α (one over k to the power α). The exponent α (alpha) says how skewed the traffic is: 0 means every key is equally popular, and bigger means more skewed. With α = 1, the share is 1/k, so the top key gets twice the traffic of the second and ten times that of the tenth. For a million shops:

| α | top 0.1% of keys | top 1% | top 10% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.6 | 6.0% of requests | 15.6% | 39.6% |
| 0.8 | 20.7% | 36.2% | 60.9% |
| 1.0 | 52.0% | 68.0% | 84.0% |
| 1.2 | 82.2% | 91.0% | 96.5% |

At α = 1, a cache that holds only 1,000 of the million shops could answer half of all lookups.

Does real traffic look like this? Twitter (now X) runs hundreds of cache clusters, groups of machines that work as one cache. Its engineers recorded every request to 153 of them for a week, about 700 billion requests in all. In 80% of the workloads (the streams of requests the clusters served), popularity fitted a Zipf distribution well, and most α values fell between 1 and 2.5. Workloads that mostly read had a typical α near 1.4, and workloads that mostly write near 0.9. So real caches are often more skewed than the classic α = 1.

Skew has a second face, the long tail: the huge number of keys that are each asked for rarely. In a million requests at α = 1, the demo below touched 217,407 different shops, and 69% of them were asked for exactly once. A cache can't help a key that never comes back, and every such key takes a slot from one that will. Expiry, eviction and memory, lesson 5 of this track, is about getting rid of those keys quickly.

So a small cache catches most requests. Next, we'll count what the ones it misses cost.

sections.h: Count the misses: why 99% hits is ten times better than 90%
sections.body:
Let's put numbers on it. The share of requests a cache answers is its **hit ratio**, often written h: the hits divided by all requests. The miss ratio is the rest, 1 − h. Two formulas tell you what a hit ratio is worth:

- average time of a lookup = h × (time of a hit) + (1 − h) × (time of a miss)
- questions reaching the slow layer each second = (1 − h) × lookups per second

Big apps run the same program on several servers at once, so that one crash doesn't stop the card readers. To share one cache, the copies keep it in Redis, a program that holds data in memory and hands it out over the network. Here are round numbers, made up for teaching but realistic. A shop lookup takes 0.5 ms from Redis and 10 ms from a busy database. At the busiest hour, the program makes 100,000 lookups a second.

| Hit ratio | Average time of a lookup | Database queries a second |
|---|---|---|
| 90% | 0.9 × 0.5 + 0.1 × 10 = 1.45 ms | 10,000 |
| 99% | 0.595 ms | 1,000 |
| 99.9% | 0.5095 ms | 100 |

From 90% to 99% looks like nine points. It's ten times fewer misses, so a tenth of the database's load, and the average lookup gets more than twice as fast. From 99% to 99.9%, the average hardly moves, because it's already close to the cache's own 0.5 ms. The database's load falls tenfold again, though. "98% hits" and "2% misses" describe the same cache, and only the second says what the database sees. **The database feels only the misses. Count them.**

At large scale, the misses are what companies build for. Meta, the company behind Facebook, runs a cache called TAO that answers more than a quadrillion (a million billion) questions a day. Even at 99% hits, it would go to the slower layer more than ten trillion times a day. Uber looked at one of its workloads, over 6 million requests a second. It estimated that the databases would need about 60,000 CPU cores without its Redis cache, against about 3,000 cores of Redis with it.

One more effect hits requests that make many lookups. Say one card payment makes 30 lookups of different keys, and each hits 99% of the time. All 30 hit only with probability 0.99^30 (0.99 multiplied by itself 30 times), about 74%. So one payment in four waits for at least one slow read. Meta once described a popular page where 1 view in 20 fetched 1,740 items or more from Memcached, another cache program. At 99.9% hits per item, such a view has only about a 17% chance of seeing no miss at all. That's how a cache with a great average still leaves many requests slow, the effect that Latency, percentiles and the tail, in the Foundations track, is about.

How big must the cache be to keep the misses low? Next, we'll measure it.

try.title: Price a cache for card lookups, by hand
steps: The program also looks up which bank gave out each card, its issuer, from the card number's first digits. A lookup in Redis takes 0.3 ms. On a miss, the program asks the issuer's own service over the internet, which takes 120 ms. The program makes 2,000 of these lookups a second.
Work out the average lookup time and the calls to the issuer each second, at 95% hits and at 99% hits. Use paper, or `jshell`, the interactive prompt that comes with Java.
One payment makes 20 lookups of different keys. At 99% hits per lookup, what share of payments meets at least one miss and waits 120 ms?
try.expect: At 95%: 0.95 × 0.3 + 0.05 × 120 = 6.3 ms on average, and 100 calls to the issuer a second. At 99%: 0.297 + 1.2 = 1.5 ms, and 20 calls a second. Four points of hit ratio cut the average fourfold and the issuer's load fivefold. With 20 lookups at 99%, 1 − 0.99^20 is about 18%: almost one payment in five pays the full 120 ms. So the slowest tenth of payments is decided by the misses, even though the average looks fine.

aside.title: If Redis is across the network too, why is it faster than the database?
aside.body: Both pay for the same round trip, about 0.1 to 0.5 ms inside a data center. The difference is the work on the other side. The database has to read a question written in SQL, the language most databases understand, and plan how to answer it. Then it finds the row through an index (a lookup table from a key to where its row is), keeps it safe from other writers, and sometimes reads the disk. Redis finds the key in a table it keeps in memory and sends the value back. The next lesson opens Redis up and measures that difference.

sections.h: How big should the cache be? Measure a miss-ratio curve
sections.body:
A bigger cache misses less, but how much less depends on the traffic. Start with the **working set**: all the different keys a program touches in a window of time, say an hour. A cache that holds the whole working set misses only on the first request for each key. Skewed traffic has no clean edge to its working set. It has a small popular group and a long tail, and each extra slot catches a little less than the one before.

To try different sizes, you need a rule for what to throw out when the cache is full. Throwing an entry out to make room is called eviction. The classic rule is **LRU**, least recently used: evict the key that has gone longest without a request. At the café, it's the barista putting back the jar nobody has reached for all morning. LRU bets that what was used recently will be used again soon, which is temporal locality turned into a rule. The stepper below runs LRU with three slots.

Now take one recorded stream of requests, called a trace, and replay it through LRU caches of several sizes. Plot the miss ratio against the size. That plot is a **miss-ratio curve**. The demo for this section does it for a million Zipf requests over 100,000 keys:

| α | 100 keys | 1,000 keys | 10,000 keys | 50,000 keys |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.8 | 93.2% | 79.5% | 53.1% | 19.6% |
| 1.0 | 70.9% | 49.3% | 26.1% | 8.4% |
| 1.2 | 39.3% | 20.4% | 8.2% | 3.6% |

Read the α = 1 row. A cache for 1% of the keys misses about half the requests. Ten times the memory only halves the misses again, and fifty times leaves 8%. The curve falls steeply, then flattens. So the right size depends on the miss ratio you need, and the skew decides what it costs. At α = 1.2, 10,000 slots do what 50,000 do at α = 1.

Curves can also have cliffs. Picture a nightly job that reads 1,001 keys in a loop, through a 1,000-key LRU cache. It misses every single time. When key 1 comes back, LRU evicted it a moment ago to make room for key 1,001. Give the cache one more slot and it never misses. Here LRU throws out, with perfect timing, exactly the key that's needed next, and lesson 5 shows eviction rules that survive a loop like this.

One property makes LRU curves easy to reason about. A bigger LRU cache always holds every key a smaller one holds, so its miss ratio can never be higher. Your lab checks that, and checks the curve you measure against a formula that predicts what LRU should do on Zipf traffic.

So far, the cache has been one box in front of one database. A real payment passes through many of them. Next, we'll count them.

try.expect: The table above is this demo's output, and both versions print the same numbers. The loop lines say `loop over 1,001 keys: cache of 1,000 misses 100%, cache of 1,001 misses 0%` and `loop over 2,000 keys: cache of 1,000 misses 100%, cache of 2,000 misses 0%`. Neither loop is better: once the loop is longer than the cache, LRU gets nothing at all, however much longer it is. A cache that kept any fixed 1,000 of the 2,000 keys and never evicted them would hit half the time on that loop. That gap is the opening for the eviction rules in lesson 5.

sections.body:
Follow one card payment and count the caches it passes on the way. A cache inside one copy of the payments program helps only that copy. Caffeine, a library for caches inside Java and Kotlin programs, is a popular choice for that kind. A shared cache, such as Redis or the older Memcached, serves every copy at once.

| Layer | What it holds | A hit saves | Where to read more |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU caches (L1, L2, L3) | 64-byte pieces of RAM | a trip to RAM, about 100 ns | this lesson |
| A cache inside the program (a map, or Caffeine) | objects in the program's own memory | a round trip over the network | lessons 5 and 6 |
| A shared cache (Redis, Memcached) | values by key, for every copy of the program | a database query | this track |
| The database's own cache (PostgreSQL's `shared_buffers`) | 8 KB pages of tables and indexes | a disk read | The buffer pool, in the Storage engines track |
| The operating system's page cache | pieces of files | a disk read | The page cache, writeback and fsync, in the Operating systems track |
| A CDN (content delivery network) | whole web pages and pictures, on machines near the user | a trip to the company's data center | not in this course |

Some layers cache the same bytes twice. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, reads its files through the operating system. So a popular page can sit in PostgreSQL's own cache, `shared_buffers`, and in the page cache at the same time.

Every layer in that table holds copies. The official shop details live in one place, the `merchants` table. It's their **system of record**, the store that holds the official version of each fact and wins every disagreement. A cached shop is **derived data**: worked out from the record, and possible to rebuild from it. What a data system is, the first lesson of the Foundations track, drew that line. The barista's picture breaks here. The milk on the counter is the milk itself. A cached shop is a copy, and when the row in the database changes, nobody tells the copy. Three rules follow, and this track keeps coming back to them.

You can lose a cache. A Redis cache that restarts empty loses no data, but every read misses until it fills again, so the database suddenly takes the full load of reads. Size the database for that, or fill the cache before it takes traffic (Caching patterns and stampedes, lesson 6).

A cache can be wrong. A TTL, a time to live after which the copy is thrown away, limits how long a copy stays wrong. Invalidation, telling the cache to drop a copy when the record changes, shortens that (lessons 6 and 7).

Never keep the only copy in a cache. Say the program writes a note in Redis that a payment has gone through, so that a retry of the same payment isn't charged twice. That note isn't a cache entry. It's the record, and it needs the settings for data that must not be lost, not the settings for a cache (lessons 5 and 8).

Next, we'll ask what changes when a whole store lives in memory, and open up Redis to see.

compare.title: An LRU map from LinkedHashMap, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LruMap.java

kotlin.title: LruMap.kt

compare.note: Both versions use the same class from Java's standard library: `LinkedHashMap`, a map that also remembers an order for its keys. The third constructor argument, `true`, makes that the order of use instead of the order of insertion. `removeEldestEntry` runs after every `put`, and returning true drops the least recently used entry. Kotlin reads `size()` as the property `size`, and needs `MutableMap.MutableEntry` in the override. Neither version is safe for several threads at once (a thread is one line of work running inside a program). Every `get` moves an entry in one shared list, so threads would need a lock, and that lock is where LRU stops scaling (lesson 5). Real programs use a cache library such as Caffeine, which handles many threads and evicts better than LRU. This map is for tests, small tools and understanding LRU.

worked.title: Size the shop cache from its miss-ratio curve

steps.say: The fraud check makes 20,000 shop lookups a second, and the shop database is comfortable at 2,000 queries a second. So the cache may miss at most 10% of lookups. There are 100,000 shops. How many must the cache hold?
Before you have real traffic to replay, model it as Zipf over 100,000 keys, and measure the curve with the lab's code. The first 200,000 requests fill the cache (they warm it up) and aren't counted.
steps.alt_code:
val trace = ZipfGenerator(100_000, 1.0, 7).trace(1_000_000)
val curve = MissRatioCurve.measure(trace, listOf(1_000, 5_000, 10_000, 20_000, 50_000), warmup = 200_000)
curve.forEach { println("${it.size} keys: miss ratio %.3f".format(it.missRatio)) }
println(MissRatioCurve.smallestSizeFor(curve, 0.10))      // 50000

steps.say: At α = 1.0, the run printed 0.493 at 1,000 keys, 0.334 at 5,000, 0.261 at 10,000, 0.187 at 20,000 and 0.084 at 50,000. So the answer is 50,000: half of all shops. The same code with α = 1.2 printed 0.082 at 10,000 keys. The skew moved the answer by a factor of five, so measure it rather than guess it.

Measure the skew from a day of request logs, the files where a program writes one line for each request it handles. Count the lookups per shop, sort the counts, and see what share the top 1% get. For 100,000 shops, about 62% means α is near 1.0, and about 85% means near 1.2.
steps.alt_code:
val counts = merchantIds.groupingBy { it }.eachCount().values.sortedDescending()
val top1 = counts.take(counts.size / 100).sum().toDouble() / merchantIds.size
println("top 1%% of merchants: %.0f%% of lookups".format(100 * top1))

steps.say: Then price it. 50,000 shop records of about 1 KB each come to about 50 MB, which is cheap, so here you'd cache all 100,000. The curve earns its keep when the data is big. For 50 million cards at 1 KB each, half of them is 50 GB, and the curve tells you whether 5 GB would already be enough.

lab.title: Make skewed traffic, build LRU and measure its miss-ratio curve
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 16 fail for now. None of them needs Docker or any other tool: this lab is plain Java and Kotlin, and the tests finish in a few seconds.

In `ZipfGenerator.kt`, write `buildCdf`, `probability` and `next`. The comment above each function lists the steps. `cdf` is a running total: its entry for key k holds the chance that one request asks for one of the top k keys. Run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l01.ZipfGeneratorTest'` until its five tests pass. One of them checks that key 1 gets 13.36% of the traffic among 1,000 keys at α = 1.

In `LruCache.java`, write `access`. The map keeps its keys in order of use, from oldest to newest, so `get` already moves a key to the newest end. Run the same command with `LruCacheTest` in place of `ZipfGeneratorTest`.

In `MissRatioCurve.kt`, write `missRatio`, `measure` and `smallestSizeFor`, then run all the tests. `MissRatioCurveTest` replays 300,000 Zipf requests. It checks your curve, to within 2 points, against Che's approximation, a formula that predicts LRU's miss ratio on this kind of traffic (see Go deeper).
Read the test `a loop one key bigger than the cache misses every time`. Predict its two numbers before you look at what it checks.
hints: In `buildCdf`, keep a running sum and store it after each addition. `probability(1)` is `cdf[0]`. For any other rank, it's `cdf[rank - 1] - cdf[rank - 2]`.

For `next`, search the sorted `cdf` by halving: start with `lo = 0` and `hi = n - 1`. While `lo < hi`, take `mid = (lo + hi) ushr 1`; if `cdf[mid] > u`, set `hi = mid`, else `lo = mid + 1`. Return `lo + 1`.
`entries.get(key) != null` is the hit test, because every value is `Boolean.TRUE`. Don't use `containsKey` for it: it doesn't move the key to the newest end.
The least recently used key is `entries.keySet().iterator().next()`. Remove it before you `put` the new key, and only when `entries.size() >= capacity`.
In `missRatio`, call `cache.resetStats()` after the warm-up loop, replay the rest, and return `cache.missRatio()`.

drill.title: Write LRU's access from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. You have a `LinkedHashMap<K, Boolean> entries` that keeps its keys in order of use (access order), and an `int capacity`. Write `boolean access(K key)`: return true on a hit. On a miss, evict the least recently used key if the cache is full, then insert the new one and return false. Then compare with the answer. Why must the hit test use `get` and not `containsKey`?

recap: Data sits on a ladder, and each rung is ten to a thousand times slower than the one above. A read takes about 1 ns from the CPU's L1 cache, 100 ns from RAM and 1 µs from a file the operating system holds in memory. A round trip takes 0.1 to 0.5 ms in a data center, and 70 ms or more to another region.

A cache keeps copies of part of the data on a faster rung. It pays because requests are skewed. With Zipf popularity at α = 1, the top 1% of a million keys get 68% of the requests, and Twitter's caches were mostly more skewed than that.
The average lookup takes h × hit time + (1 − h) × miss time, and the slow layer sees (1 − h) × requests. Going from 90% to 99% hits cuts its load tenfold, so count the misses, not the hits.
A request that makes n lookups sees no miss with probability h^n, which is why requests with many lookups feel the misses even when the average looks good.
A miss-ratio curve, from replaying one stream of requests through caches of several sizes, says what each extra slot buys. On Zipf traffic it falls fast, then flattens.

The limit: a cache is only a copy. Lose it and the database takes every read, and it can be out of date. It can't help keys that never come back, LRU gets nothing from a loop longer than the cache, and it must never hold the only copy of anything.
closing:
We started with a barista's jug of milk and a program that asks the database about the same shops all day. A small copy close by catches most of those lookups, because a few shops get most of them, and the misses that remain decide how hard the database works.

Open any web page twice with your browser's developer tools showing the Network tab. On the second load, many files come from the cache almost instantly. The rest are the misses, and they decide how long the page takes.

Next, we'll open up Redis, a store that keeps all its data in memory, and see how it serves thousands of programs at once, doing one thing at a time.

quiz.q: One card payment makes 50 cache lookups, each for a different key. Each lookup finds its copy 99% of the time, independently of the others. About what share of payments meets at least one miss?
options: About 40%
quiz.why: All 50 hit with probability 0.99^50, about 0.61, so about 39% of payments wait for at least one slow read. 1% is the miss ratio of one lookup, not of a payment that makes fifty. That's why requests with many lookups feel the misses even when the hit ratio looks excellent.

quiz.q: A million cards are each looked up about equally often: no card is more popular than any other. The cache holds 100,000 of them. Roughly what hit ratio can it reach once it's full?
options: About 10%
About 50%
About 84%, as with Zipf traffic at α = 1
Close to 100%, once it has been running a while
quiz.why: With no skew, every card is equally likely to be the next request, so a cache holding 10% of them hits about 10% of the time, whichever 10% it keeps. 84% is what the top 10% of keys get under Zipf with α = 1, and that needs skew. Waiting doesn't help either: there are no popular keys to hold on to.

quiz.q: A cache's hit ratio rises from 95% to 99%. What happens to the number of questions reaching the database behind it?
options: It falls by about 4%
It falls by about half
It stays the same; only the speed changes
It falls to a fifth
quiz.why: The database only hears about the misses. They fall from 5% of requests to 1%, so the database gets a fifth of the questions it got before. Reading the change as four points of hit ratio hides that, which is why it pays to count misses per second.

quiz.q: A nightly job reads the same 1.2 million account keys in the same order, again and again, through an LRU cache that holds 1 million keys. After the first pass, about what hit ratio does the job get?
options: About 83%, the share of keys that fit
About 0%
About 50%
quiz.why: When a key comes back, 1.2 million minus one other keys have been read since. LRU has room for only 1 million, so that key was evicted shortly before it was needed. Every request misses. 83% is what a cache would get if it kept a fixed 1 million keys and never evicted them. LRU's rule, evict the key unused for longest, is exactly wrong for a loop larger than the cache.

quiz.q: The Redis cache in front of the shop database restarts and comes back empty. What happens?
options: The shop details are lost until someone restores a backup
Nothing: the program reads from a copy of the database instead
No data is lost, but every lookup misses until the cache fills, so the database takes the full load of reads for a while
Redis loads the shops from the database by itself when it starts
quiz.why: A cache holds derived data, so the `merchants` table still has everything. But the cache was answering 99% of the reads, so for a while the database sees up to a hundred times its usual reads. Redis never loads anything from your database by itself: the program fills it on misses (Caching patterns and stampedes, lesson 6).

flashcards.front: What's the average lookup time of a cache with hit ratio h?
flashcards.back: h × hit time + (1 − h) × miss time. With 0.5 ms hits and 10 ms misses, that's 1.45 ms at 90% and 0.595 ms at 99%.

flashcards.front: Why is 99% hits ten times better than 90% for the database?
flashcards.back: The database only hears about the misses: 1% of requests instead of 10%.

flashcards.front: What does a Zipf distribution with α = 1 say about popularity?
flashcards.back: The key ranked k gets requests in proportion to 1/k. Key 1 gets twice the traffic of key 2 and ten times that of key 10.

flashcards.front: What did Twitter's study of 153 cache clusters find about popularity?
flashcards.back: 80% of the workloads fitted Zipf well, with α mostly between 1 and 2.5: more skewed than the classic α = 1.
The miss ratio of one stream of requests, replayed through caches of different sizes. It shows what each extra slot buys.

flashcards.front: When does an LRU cache miss every request?
flashcards.back: When requests loop over more keys than it holds: each key is evicted shortly before it comes back.

flashcards.front: Why is a cache derived data?
flashcards.back: It holds copies worked out from a system of record. You can throw it away and rebuild it, and it can be out of date.

terms.plain: A smaller, faster store that keeps copies of some of the data from a bigger, slower one.
Hits divided by all requests. The miss ratio is one minus it.
The habit of programs to reuse data they used recently (temporal) and data next to it (spatial).
Popularity where the key ranked k gets a share in proportion to 1/k^α. A bigger α means more skew.
All the different keys a program touches in a window of time.
The miss ratio of one stream of requests, plotted against the size of the cache.
Least recently used: when the cache is full, evict the key that has gone longest without a request.
Data worked out from a system of record, such as a cache or an index. It can be rebuilt from the record.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Our shop cache hits 98% of the time, so there's nothing left to gain, and doubling its memory would be a waste." Explain what you'd check before you agree.
explain_back.answer: 98% hits means 2% misses, and the misses are what the database and the slow requests feel. First I'd turn it into numbers. At 20,000 lookups a second, 2% is 400 database queries a second. With 0.5 ms hits and 10 ms misses, the average is about 0.69 ms, while 99.5% would give about 0.55 ms and only 100 queries a second. Then I'd look at requests that make many lookups. A payment that makes 30 lookups at 98% meets at least one miss about 45% of the time, and those payments are the slow ones. Whether more memory helps is a question for the miss-ratio curve. I'd replay a day of real lookups through simulated caches of today's size and of twice that. Skewed traffic gives a curve that flattens, so doubling might take the misses from 2% to 1.5% or to 0.5%, and only the measurement says which. Last, I'd check what the misses are. If most are first requests for keys that never come back, no amount of memory removes them.

deeper.body:
The lab checks your LRU against a formula. **Che's approximation** (Che, Tung and Wang, 2002) describes LRU when every request is drawn independently of the others. It uses one number T, the characteristic time: how many requests it takes for C different keys to be asked for, where C is the cache size. A key with request probability p is in the cache if it was requested within the last T requests, which happens with probability 1 − e^(−pT). Solve Σ(1 − e^(−p_i·T)) = C for T, and the hit ratio is Σ p_i·(1 − e^(−p_i·T)). For 100,000 keys at α = 1 and 1,000 slots, it predicts 49.4% misses, and the demo measured 49.3%. It assumes every request is drawn independently, so it knows nothing about loops, bursts, or a key that's popular for an hour and then never again.

You don't have to replay a trace once for every size. Because a bigger LRU cache holds everything a smaller one holds, Mattson and colleagues at IBM showed in 1970 that one pass computes the whole curve. For each request, count how many different keys were used since the last request for the same key: its stack distance. A cache of size C hits exactly the requests whose stack distance is below C. Real systems sample to keep that cheap. SHARDS (Waldspurger and colleagues, FAST 2015) hashes each key and keeps only a small, fixed fraction of the keys, and still gets curves close to the full ones.

The loop in the first Try it visited the array in a random cycle on purpose. Walk the same 256 MB array in order and each read gets far cheaper. The CPU fetches 64 bytes at a time, and when it sees a pattern, it loads the next pieces before they're asked for (prefetching). That's spatial locality doing its job. The random cycle defeats both, which is why it shows the raw cost of going to RAM.

In a running system, watch misses per second, not the hit ratio alone. Redis reports its count of misses as `keyspace_misses` in the output of its `INFO stats` command, and Caffeine counts them when a cache is built with `recordStats()`.

The split between systems of record and derived data opens *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 1, which counts caches, indexes and materialized views as derived data. Materialized views and data cubes, in the Storage engines track, built one of the others from scratch.
